<main>
<div class="page page-article reveal">
  <a href="../insights.html" class="arrow-link article-back">← Insights</a>

  <div class="eyebrow page-eyebrow">Customer Analytics · Case Study</div>
  <h1 class="page-title">The sure thing problem</h1>
  <p class="article-deck">
    A mobile game had proof its ads worked — conversion more than doubled in a clean
    experiment. The harder question was <em>who</em> to keep showing them to. Ranking players by who
    was most likely to buy turned out to be the expensive answer.
  </p>

  <dl class="article-meta">
    <div><dt>Role</dt><dd>Analyst</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Case</dt><dd>Mobile game ad targeting</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Stack</dt><dd>Python · polars · pyrsm · scikit-learn</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Course</dt><dd>MGTA 455, Rady School of Management</dd></div>
  </dl>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>The setup</h2>
    <p>A studio behind a successful mobile action game launched its first paid expansion at
    <strong>$14.99</strong>. Two months in, only <strong>5.75%</strong> of active players had bought it.
    Leadership saw two possible explanations: the price was too high, or players simply didn't know the
    expansion existed.</p>
    <p>Cutting price is close to irreversible, so the awareness theory got tested first — with in-app
    ads. Showing a player ads for two weeks costs about <strong>$1.50</strong> in forgone in-game
    currency purchases. That gives the whole problem a clean economic spine: an ad is worth showing
    only when it moves someone across the line by more than $1.50 ÷ $14.99, or about
    <strong>10 percentage points</strong> of purchase probability.</p>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>The experiment worked. That was the easy part.</h2>
    <p>Two randomly assigned groups of 30,000 players each — one saw ads, one didn't:</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-stats">
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">5.69%</div><div class="article-stat-l">Conversion without ads</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">13.04%</div><div class="article-stat-l">Conversion with ads</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">+7.36pp</div><div class="article-stat-l">Absolute lift</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">+129%</div><div class="article-stat-l">Relative lift</div></div>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <p>Before trusting any of that, I checked the randomization held. Average player level came in at
    6.22 versus 6.32 between groups; friend counts at 49.8 versus 51.0; spaceship ownership 71.5%
    versus 70.3%. Every feature landed inside a few percent. The groups were comparable, so the gap in
    conversion is the ads and not the players.</p>

    <div class="article-callout">
      <p>Ads work <em>on average</em>. But you don't run a campaign on an average — you run it on a
      list. Averages hide the fact that a single number is hiding four completely different kinds of
      player.</p>
    </div>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>Four kinds of player</h2>
    <p>Every player falls into one of four boxes, depending on what they'd do with the ad and what
    they'd do without it. Only one box is worth paying for.</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-panel">
    <div class="article-panel-head">
      <div>
        <div class="article-panel-title">Who is actually worth $1.50?</div>
        <div class="article-panel-sub">Select a group to see what targeting it does to the campaign. Conceptual
        framing — not measured segment sizes.</div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="article-qaxis">↓ Buys when shown an ad &nbsp;·&nbsp; → Buys when shown nothing</div>
    <div class="article-quad" id="quad">
      <button class="article-qcell" data-q="0" aria-pressed="true">
        <div class="article-qn">Sure Things</div><div class="article-qd">Buys either way</div></button>
      <button class="article-qcell" data-q="1" aria-pressed="false">
        <div class="article-qn">Persuadables</div><div class="article-qd">Buys only if shown the ad</div></button>
      <button class="article-qcell" data-q="2" aria-pressed="false">
        <div class="article-qn">Sleeping Dogs</div><div class="article-qd">Buys only if left alone</div></button>
      <button class="article-qcell" data-q="3" aria-pressed="false">
        <div class="article-qn">Lost Causes</div><div class="article-qd">Never buys</div></button>
    </div>
    <div class="article-qout" id="qout"></div>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <p>A propensity model ranks players by <em>P(buy | ad)</em>. That score is high for Persuadables —
    but it's just as high for Sure Things, who were going to buy anyway. Spend $1.50 on a Sure Thing and
    you bought a conversion you already had.</p>
    <p>An uplift model ranks by the difference instead: <em>P(buy | ad) − P(buy | no ad)</em>. Sure Things
    score near zero, because the ad changes nothing for them. Only Persuadables rise to the top.</p>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>What the models actually returned</h2>
    <p>I built both approaches — propensity and uplift — across four algorithms, then measured
    incremental profit on an 18,000-player holdout, scaled to the full 120,000-player base.</p>
    <p>The toggle below is the finding. It switches between sending ads to a fixed top 25% of players,
    and letting each model choose its own depth using the $1.50 ÷ $14.99 threshold.</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-panel">
    <div class="article-panel-head">
      <div>
        <div class="article-panel-title">Incremental profit by model and targeting strategy</div>
        <div class="article-panel-sub" id="csub"></div>
      </div>
      <div class="article-seg" role="group" aria-label="Targeting depth">
        <button id="btn-opt" aria-pressed="true">Optimal depth</button>
        <button id="btn-fix" aria-pressed="false">Fixed 25%</button>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="article-legend">
      <div class="article-lg"><span class="article-sw" style="background:var(--s-prop)"></span>Propensity targeting</div>
      <div class="article-lg"><span class="article-sw" style="background:var(--s-up)"></span>Uplift targeting</div>
    </div>
    <div class="article-chart-host">
      <div class="article-chart-scroll"><svg id="chart" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"
        aria-label="Grouped bar chart of incremental profit by model, comparing propensity and uplift targeting"></svg></div>
      <div class="article-tip" id="tip"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="article-tbl-wrap">
      <table class="article-table"><thead><tr><th>Model</th><th>Propensity</th><th>Uplift</th><th>Difference</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody id="tbody"></tbody></table>
    </div>
    <p class="article-fine" id="precnote" hidden>≈ Values recorded to five significant figures in the original
    output; the logistic pair and all differences are exact.</p>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <p>At a <strong>fixed 25%</strong>, the story looks inconsistent. The three flexible models show
    uplift winning by $735K–$783K. Logistic regression does the opposite — its uplift version returns
    $657,986 against $1,546,217 for propensity, an $888,231 loss. Read that column alone and uplift modeling looks
    unreliable.</p>
    <p>Let each model pick its own depth and the contradiction disappears. <strong>Uplift wins for all
    four</strong>, logistic included, by $386K to $499K. The best combination — gradient boosting on
    uplift scores, 30% of players — returns <strong>$2,893,786</strong>.</p>

    <div class="article-callout">
      <p>The logistic anomaly was never really about logistic regression. It was about forcing every
      model to target the same 25%. Depth was a free parameter I'd accidentally frozen, and freezing it
      produced a finding that wasn't there.</p>
    </div>

    <p>There's a second pattern worth noticing. Propensity models want a wider audience — their optima
    land at 30% to 40% — while uplift models converge tightly on 25% to 30%. Uplift makes more money
    while mailing fewer people, which is what you'd expect once Sure Things stop occupying slots at the
    top of the list.</p>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>The technical layer</h2>
    <div class="article-tech-label">For readers who want the mechanics</div>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>How the uplift score is built</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>I used the two-model approach. One model is fit on the treated group and one on the control
    group, using the same feature set — telemetry like level reached, days active, friend count, prior
    purchases, badges earned, and device type. Each player in the holdout gets scored by both.</p>
    <p>The uplift score is the difference between those two predictions. Propensity is just the first
    prediction on its own. Both rankings come from the same fitted models, so the comparison isolates
    the <em>ranking rule</em> rather than confounding it with model quality.</p>
    <p>The known weakness: subtracting two estimates adds their errors. When both models are noisy, the
    difference is noisier than either — which is exactly why the linear model struggled at fixed depth
    while the flexible models didn't.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>Where the 10.01% threshold comes from</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>Showing ads costs $1.50; a conversion is worth $14.99. Targeting a player pays off when expected
    incremental revenue clears the cost:</p>
    <p><strong>uplift × $14.99 &gt; $1.50</strong>, so <strong>uplift &gt; 0.1001</strong></p>
    <p>Count how many holdout players clear that bar and you get the optimal depth directly from the
    data rather than from a round number. Those counts came to 24.23% for logistic uplift, 31.26% for
    the neural network, 31.46% for random forest, and 31.14% for gradient boosting — each rounded to the
    nearest 5% for a deployable rule.</p>
    <p>The same threshold applies to propensity scores, but it means something different there: it asks
    whether someone is likely to buy at all, not whether the ad is what moved them. Same arithmetic,
    different question — and that difference is the entire post.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>Validating the implementation across two libraries</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>I built every model twice — once through the course's <code>pyrsm</code> wrapper, once directly
    in scikit-learn — then correlated the predictions to check the pipeline.</p>
    <p>Random forest agreed almost perfectly (0.999 on treatment predictions, 0.995 on uplift), and
    gradient boosting nearly as closely (0.975 / 0.979). The neural network came in far lower, at 0.595
    and 0.541.</p>
    <p>That gap isn't a bug — neural networks are sensitive to initialization, solver, and learning-rate
    schedule, and the two libraries don't share defaults. But it is a caution: the neural network's
    numbers are the least reproducible in the set, and I'd want a fixed seed and a matched optimizer
    before putting weight on them.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>What I'd do differently</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p><strong>Report a range, not a point.</strong> Every profit figure is a single draw on one 18,000-row
    holdout. Two of the four differences fall within a few hundred thousand dollars of each other on a
    $2.8M base. Bootstrapped intervals would show which gaps survive resampling — my guess is the
    uplift-versus-propensity gap does, and the ranking among the three flexible models does not.</p>
    <p><strong>Check the Sleeping Dogs empirically.</strong> The framing above assumes they exist, but I
    never tested the bottom of the uplift distribution for genuinely negative treatment effects. If ads
    actively suppress purchases for some players, that's a finding worth having on its own.</p>
    <p><strong>Model the depth decision directly.</strong> Rounding 31.14% to 30% is defensible, but the
    profit curve near the optimum is flat enough that the rounding could matter more than the model
    choice. I'd plot profit across every decile before committing.</p>
    </div>
    </details>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>What this case taught me</h2>
    <p>The transferable lesson isn't "use uplift models." It's that <strong>the metric you rank on
    encodes a causal claim</strong>, whether or not you meant to make one. Ranking by <em>who will
    convert</em> quietly assumes the treatment caused the conversion. Ranking by <em>who will convert
    because of the ad</em> makes that assumption explicit and testable.</p>
    <p>The second lesson is cheaper to state and easier to forget: a comparison is only as honest as the
    parameters you held fixed. I nearly drew a conclusion about logistic regression that was
    really a conclusion about my own choice of 25%.</p>
    <div class="chips article-chips">
      <span class="chip">Uplift / CATE modeling</span>
      <span class="chip">Randomized experiment validation</span>
      <span class="chip">Profit-based decision thresholds</span>
      <span class="chip">Gradient boosting</span>
      <span class="chip">Neural networks</span>
      <span class="chip">Random forests</span>
      <span class="chip">Holdout evaluation</span>
      <span class="chip">polars</span>
      <span class="chip">scikit-learn</span>
    </div>
    <p class="article-fine">Figures are from my own analysis on the course dataset. The underlying case materials
    and data are proprietary to the publisher and are not reproduced here.</p>
  </section>
</div>

<script>
  const io = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
    entries.forEach(e => { if (e.isIntersecting) e.target.classList.add('visible'); });
  }, { threshold: 0.08 });
  document.querySelectorAll('.reveal').forEach(el => io.observe(el));

  (function(){
    var DATA={
      opt:{
        sub:"Each model targets the depth its own threshold implies. Holdout results scaled to 120,000 players.",
        rows:[
          {m:"Logistic",       p:1824659, u:2298288, pp:30, up:25, d:473629, exact:true},
          {m:"Neural Net",     p:2367532, u:2821018, pp:35, up:30, d:453486, exact:true},
          {m:"Random Forest",  p:2459369, u:2845375, pp:40, up:30, d:386006, exact:true},
          {m:"Gradient Boost", p:2395171, u:2893786, pp:35, up:30, d:498614, exact:true}
        ]},
      fix:{
        sub:"Every model forced to the same top 25% of players — the comparison that produced a misleading result.",
        approx:true,
        rows:[
          {m:"Logistic",       p:1546217, u:657986,  pp:25, up:25, d:-888231, exact:true},
          {m:"Neural Net",     p:1953900, u:2736700, pp:25, up:25, d:782771},
          {m:"Random Forest",  p:2016000, u:2750500, pp:25, up:25, d:734531},
          {m:"Gradient Boost", p:2007200, u:2747500, pp:25, up:25, d:740307}
        ]}
    };
    var mode="opt";
    var svg=document.getElementById("chart"), tip=document.getElementById("tip"),
        tbody=document.getElementById("tbody"), csub=document.getElementById("csub"),
        host=svg.parentNode.parentNode;
    var W=760,H=400,ML=72,MR=16,MT=32,MB=74,YMAX=3.1e6;
    function money(v,ex){return (ex?"":"\u2248")+"$"+Math.round(v).toLocaleString("en-US");}
    function mshort(v){return "$"+(v/1e6).toFixed(2)+"M";}
    function el(n,a){var e=document.createElementNS("http://www.w3.org/2000/svg",n);
      for(var k in a)e.setAttribute(k,a[k]);return e;}

    function draw(){
      var d=DATA[mode],rows=d.rows;
      csub.textContent=d.sub;
      while(svg.firstChild)svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
      var pw=W-ML-MR, ph=H-MT-MB, y=function(v){return MT+ph-(v/YMAX)*ph;};

      for(var t=0;t<=3e6;t+=5e5){
        svg.appendChild(el("line",{x1:ML,x2:W-MR,y1:y(t),y2:y(t),stroke:"var(--grid)","stroke-width":1}));
        var yl=el("text",{x:ML-11,y:y(t)+4,"text-anchor":"end","class":"article-ax"});
        yl.textContent=t===0?"$0":"$"+(t/1e6).toFixed(1)+"M";
        svg.appendChild(yl);
      }
      var gw=pw/rows.length;
      rows.forEach(function(r,i){
        var cx=ML+gw*i+gw/2, bw=Math.min(52,gw*0.29), gap=2;
        [["p",r.p,"var(--s-prop)","Propensity",r.pp],["u",r.u,"var(--s-up)","Uplift",r.up]]
        .forEach(function(s,j){
          var v=s[1], bx=cx+(j===0?-bw-gap/2:gap/2), bh=Math.max(2,MT+ph-y(v));
          var bar=el("rect",{x:bx,y:y(v),width:bw,height:bh,rx:4,fill:s[2],"class":"bar"});
          bar.addEventListener("mouseenter",function(){
            bar.classList.add("on");
            tip.innerHTML="<b>"+r.m+" · "+s[3]+"</b><br><span class='article-tip-num'>"+money(v)+
              "</span><br>targets top "+s[4]+"% of players";
            tip.style.opacity=1;
            var hb=host.getBoundingClientRect(),bb=bar.getBoundingClientRect();
            var lx=bb.left-hb.left+bb.width/2-tip.offsetWidth/2;
            tip.style.left=Math.max(4,Math.min(lx,hb.width-tip.offsetWidth-4))+"px";
            tip.style.top=(bb.top-hb.top-tip.offsetHeight-9)+"px";
          });
          bar.addEventListener("mouseleave",function(){bar.classList.remove("on");tip.style.opacity=0;});
          svg.appendChild(bar);
          var vl=el("text",{x:bx+bw/2,y:y(v)-7,"text-anchor":"middle","class":"article-vlab"});
          vl.textContent=mshort(v); svg.appendChild(vl);
        });
        var ml=el("text",{x:cx,y:MT+ph+21,"text-anchor":"middle","class":"article-mlab"});
        ml.textContent=r.m; svg.appendChild(ml);
        var diff=r.d, sign=diff>=0?"+":"−";
        var dl=el("text",{x:cx,y:MT+ph+40,"text-anchor":"middle","class":"article-dlab",
          fill:diff>=0?"var(--s-up)":"var(--s-prop)"});
        dl.textContent=sign+"$"+Math.abs(Math.round(diff)).toLocaleString("en-US")+" uplift";
        svg.appendChild(dl);
        var dp=el("text",{x:cx,y:MT+ph+55,"text-anchor":"middle","class":"article-ax"});
        dp.textContent=mode==="opt"?("targets "+r.pp+"% vs "+r.up+"%"):"both at 25%";
        svg.appendChild(dp);
      });
      svg.appendChild(el("line",{x1:ML,x2:W-MR,y1:MT+ph,y2:MT+ph,stroke:"var(--line-2)","stroke-width":1}));
      var yt=el("text",{x:ML,y:MT-12,"text-anchor":"start","class":"article-ax"});
      yt.textContent="Incremental profit"; svg.appendChild(yt);

      tbody.innerHTML=rows.map(function(r){
        var diff=r.d;
        return "<tr><td>"+r.m+"</td><td>"+money(r.p,r.exact)+"</td><td>"+money(r.u,r.exact)+"</td><td>"+
          (diff>=0?"+":"−")+"$"+Math.abs(Math.round(diff)).toLocaleString("en-US")+"</td></tr>";
      }).join("");
    }
    function setMode(m){
      mode=m;
      document.getElementById("btn-opt").setAttribute("aria-pressed",m==="opt");
      document.getElementById("btn-fix").setAttribute("aria-pressed",m==="fix");
      draw();
      document.getElementById('precnote').hidden = (m!=='fix');
    }
    document.getElementById("btn-opt").addEventListener("click",function(){setMode("opt");});
    document.getElementById("btn-fix").addEventListener("click",function(){setMode("fix");});
    setMode("opt");

    var Q=[
     "<strong>Sure Things won't notice.</strong> They were always going to buy. Every $1.50 spent here is pure waste — and because their purchase probability is high, a propensity model puts them at the very top of the list.",
     "<strong>Persuadables are the whole business case.</strong> The ad is the reason they convert. This is the only group where $1.50 buys something that wouldn't have happened, and it's the group an uplift score is built to find.",
     "<strong>Sleeping Dogs get worse when contacted.</strong> The ad actively pushes them away. A propensity model can't see this at all; an uplift model scores them negative and drops them to the bottom, where they belong.",
     "<strong>Lost Causes are cheap to skip.</strong> Nothing converts them, so both approaches correctly rank them low. They're the one group that's easy to get right."
    ];
    var qout=document.getElementById("qout"), cells=document.querySelectorAll(".article-qcell");
    function pick(i){
      cells.forEach(function(c){c.setAttribute("aria-pressed",+c.dataset.q===i);});
      qout.innerHTML=Q[i];
    }
    cells.forEach(function(c){c.addEventListener("click",function(){pick(+c.dataset.q);});});
    pick(0);
  })();
</script>
